name: Erik Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sell homes for Northgate Homes, a small independent agency with six of us in a commuter town about forty minutes from the city. A normal day is two valuations in the morning, a few viewings after lunch, then chasing buyers' solicitors until about six. I use AI tools all day, honestly: I draft listings with one, I have another pull recent sales for a valuation, and I let it sort my inbox before I've had coffee. I love the moment a first-time buyer gets the keys, and I hate when a chain of five sales falls apart because of one survey.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI all day. Did the agency ask you to?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, I just started doing it and then showed the owner, Diane, what it saved. Now she pays for two of the tools. I'm not the best salesman in the office, I'm pretty average at the closing bit, but I'm the one who sorts the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but they were never going to replace an agent, and I'd say it a bit smugly. At work I'd keep pushing the ones that actually save time. Online I'd post something about how the money that went into AI hype could have built a lot of social housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I like the tools and I'd hoped they'd take the boring half of the job off me completely. But my job's safe, my pay is good, and that's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got and maybe build a better valuation template for the office. I'd keep my savings ticking over, about ten months now plus some index funds. I'd probably start studying for the property management certificate, just so I've got more than sales on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe. My life is fine in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned social housing. Does your work bump into that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time. I do viewings with couples on two good salaries who still can't afford a two-bed terrace on Mill Lane. I make commission off a market that's broken for people my age, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you square that, being progressive and earning from a broken market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very well, if I'm honest. I vote for building more homes and I donate to a housing charity every month. I also need the commission, and I'm good at being nice to people on a hard day.

say: I'd say the tools are useful but **never replaced agents**.
I'd post that AI hype money could have built **social housing** instead.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed** the tools didn't take the boring half of the job.
My **job and pay** are safe, which is worth a lot.
do: Build a better **valuation template** for the office.
Keep **ten months** of savings and index funds ticking over.
Start the **property management certificate** to widen his CV.
S0.quote: I make commission off a market that's broken for people my age, and I know it.
fieldNote: He is the office's **tech person**, but admits to being **average** at closing deals.
He openly names the **tension** between his values and his commission.
Disappointment, not relief, is his reaction to **AI stalling**.

steps.text: Build a valuation template from recent sales for the office
Start the property management certificate this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where agents who learn the tools do well and agents who don't struggle. At work I'd offer to train everyone, including Diane. Online I'd say the savings should go into shorter hours for staff, not just bigger margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I'm already doing half of what the card describes, so I'd be the one other people come to. The risk is that one negotiator with good tools can cover what two did, and we're a small office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd write up how each tool fits into our process and run a Friday session for the team. I'd ask Diane for a pay rise tied to the time I'm saving the office, because that's real money. Later in the year I'd look at becoming the person who sets this up for other small agencies, maybe as a side business at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with a bit of guilt mixed in. I'd be helping bring in the thing that might cost Martin his job. Martin's our office junior, and he's twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say that to Martin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd tell him to learn the tools with me, because the junior job that's mostly answering the phone is the first to go. Martin could be the one running the system in two years. I'd rather he hears that from me than from a restructure email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side business actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something simple, like setting up inboxes, listing templates and valuation tools for small agencies, charging a few hundred pounds each. There must be a hundred tiny agencies in our county with one person who hates computers. I'd do it Saturdays until it either worked or didn't.

I'd argue savings should fund **shorter hours** for staff.
think: I think it's **good for me**, as I already do half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and the government needs to put money in people's hands fast. At work I'd be straight with everyone that the office will shrink. Online I'd back a tax on AI firms to pay for retraining and support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my edge disappears. Being the tech guy only matters while the tech needs a guy. If AI can value, write, negotiate and chase solicitors better than me by 2028, Diane needs maybe one person to do viewings and sign things until the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd move more of my savings into index funds and keep a full year in cash. I'd talk to Diane about becoming that one person, and I'd be honest that it might be her and not me. In the first year after it lands I'd try to move into whatever's left that's human, like the housing co-op my friend runs, where people still want someone to sit in meetings and sort things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, which surprises me a bit. I always thought I'd be fine because I'm early with the tech. But early with the tech doesn't help when the tech doesn't need you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means viewings and keys are mine for a while. That's maybe a third of the week. So I'd have a job, but a smaller, worse-paid one, without the commission from the bit I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Lena's a graphic designer, so she'd be hit at the same time, maybe sooner. We'd have the money talk at the kitchen table that night. I'd say we're okay for a year and then we'd have to be clever.

say: I'd say we're **not ready** and the government must get money to people fast.
I'd back **a tax** on AI firms to fund retraining.
think: I think **my edge disappears** once the tech no longer needs a tech guy.

Look for roles at his friend's **housing co-op**.
feel: He feels **anxious**, surprised his tech head start **doesn't help**.

fieldNote: His confidence **flips** in the fast scenario.

steps.text: Move part of savings into index funds and keep a year in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but enough to do this properly if the government acts now. At work I'd push Diane to plan the transition instead of waiting. Online I'd write about how small agencies can share tools so the big chains don't swallow them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives me time to turn the side business into something real before AGI makes it pointless. I'd also get the property management certificate, because looking after buildings and tenants needs more people than selling them. It's not safe, but it's a few good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the Saturday tool setup business in year one and try to get ten agencies signed up. I'd do the property management certificate by evening classes. And I'd keep our cash reserve at a year, because Lena and I would want a cushion for when it actually lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd have a plan, and I like having a plan. I'd still not love the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the side business worth it if AGI makes it pointless in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Two or three years of good money teaches me to run something, and that's worth more than being the sixth person in a six-person office. Even if it dies, the skills don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots three years after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2034 the viewing part goes too, I guess. That's when I'd want to be in property management or in the co-op, doing the people bits nobody's figured out how to automate. I'd be 35, so I'd have time.

I'd write about small agencies **sharing tools** against the big chains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time if people use it, and I'd tell everyone to start now. At work I'd keep pushing the tools. Online I'd be arguing for public investment in housing, since a lot of people will need cheaper homes when their careers change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Ten years is enough to build something, learn property management and still be young when the robots arrive. I'd be 37 at AGI and 40 when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling and keep pushing the tools at Northgate for the next few years. I'd grow the side business slowly and maybe buy a small flat to let, if Lena's up for it. And I'd keep putting money into index funds every month, because AI firms might be where the growth is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. It's the version where I get to be early and still have time to change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a flat to let. Does that sit with your views on housing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two-thirds of my friends rent from someone. I'd rather it was someone like me who fixes the boiler the same day. I know that's a bit of a convenient argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change course in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw agencies shrinking faster than the card says, I'd move into property management earlier. I'd watch our own office numbers, because if Diane stops hiring juniors that's the sign. I don't need to guess, I'll see it.

I'd argue for **public investment** in housing for people changing careers.

I'd be **37 at AGI** and 40 when the robots come.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the one advantage I've built and hits Lena's job at the same time. What would help is something like a year of income support while you retrain, funded by the AI firms making the money. I don't need much, I just need time to land somewhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the person bringing the tools in. I like bringing the tools in, but I'm also the reason the office needs fewer people. I'd want the people I train to get something out of it too, not just Diane's margins.

headlineQuote: I like bringing the tools in, but I'm also the reason the office needs fewer people.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old sales negotiator** at a six-person independent agency, and its unofficial tech person.
He's progressive and uneasy about **earning commission** from a housing market his friends can't afford.
He stays calm in slow scenarios but grows **anxious** when AGI arrives fast and his edge vanishes.
With more time he plans **a side business**, property management study and some investing.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, which wipes out his edge and hits his partner's design job too.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a year of **income support** for retraining, funded by AI firms.
